One of the problems with projects like Physlib is scalability of reviews. Basically the question is: How do you scale reviews with contributions.

Some solutions I know of doing this are:

  1. Lower the quality of reviews.
  2. Automate reviews using an AI.
  3. Make reviews a requirement to getting PRs merged (e.g. one review per contribution).

I don't really like any of these. I'm sure this is not a problem just the Lean community faces, so I was wondering if anyone knows of other solutions to this problem?
(Maybe it is just a case of having good infrastructure)

Just a suggestion but maybe the team of maintainers could establish a reviewing_guidelines.md?

I really want to help with reviewing process but I often get kind of lost (and maybe I'm not alone). It will be incredibly helpful if we could get an outline of what to look for in peer review, how to leave constructive comments on formatting and style, and most importantly the global constraints of the project that a newcomer might not be aware of. There maybe many more things I'm missing but I think this would be a great start to get more people into the review process.

We have this: https://github.com/leanprover-community/physlib/blob/master/docs/ReviewGuidelines.md, this doesn't cover everything you mention, but it is part of the way.

In terms of global constraints, do you have an example of what you are thinking of?

Sorry, on reflection I think that message was negligent on my part, I should've actually read through ReviewGuidelines.md before commenting, and it does cover more than I gave it credit for.

Thinking about it more, what I actually had in mind by "global constraints" was project scope/direction decisions for each of the different areas of physics the project is covering so that reviews have a common ground for each topic tag (similar to using L&L and Wilde as scope), however I don't know if this is something you can easily write down at the moment.

Additionally I do think that getting better at reviewing is mostly a matter of just doing more reviews on the areas of expertise we have :)

Thinking about it more, what I actually had in mind by "global constraints" was project scope/direction decisions for each of the different areas of physics the project is covering so that reviews have a common ground for each topic tag (similar to using L&L and Wilde as scope), however I don't know if this is something you can easily write down at the moment.

My hope is that the API-maps discussed here will in the end correspond to this.

I generally think we should work on the philosophy that investments to lower the hurdle for the collective to work/review on the project are very important. (So e.g. if ReviewerGuidlines.md can be made any better, then I think we should spend the time making it better).
Maybe one thing we could do is make a reviewer checklist, if people think that would help?
Mhmm yes I think that would be great, I would begin using it immediately.

Hi there, I am back.

I think the solution to this problem has two aspects.
The first is making sure everyone's PRs are well-formed and conform to our standards. We could achieve this by having everyone submit PRs through our Physlib AI tool, where the AI guides the user toward producing pull requests that meet our conventions and are high quality from the start.
The second is having the AI review these pull requests: for simpler PRs the AI can approve them directly, while for cases where it's less certain or the PR is more complex, it can hand off to a human for further review.

Another approach would be to designate around 10 people to each take responsibility for one of 10 different areas. We could motivate them by granting titles that recognize their role and encourage engagement. If someone becomes inactive due to their own work or steps back after a certain period, we can rotate in someone else to replace them.

Since any contributor can review a PR, an auto PR should be reviewed by the contributor making it? And the maintainers can then just merge it? This will ensure the contributor is maintaining quality of PRs being raised by their LLMs??

(Sorry just realised cannot review own account PR even if it's by an LLM as discussed in morning)

Jinzheng Li said:

Another approach would be to designate around 10 people to each take responsibility for one of 10 different areas. We could motivate them by granting titles that recognize their role and encourage engagement. If someone becomes inactive due to their own work or steps back after a certain period, we can rotate in someone else to replace them.

Maybe we could make a role of Reviewer in addition to Maintainer for which entry is metric based. E.g.

  • After 10 good reviews and 10 good contributions to an area X one becomes a reviewer of area X. (At the discretion of the maintainers to ensure people don't game the system).
  • One retains reviewer status on area X if over the course of every calendar month one does 3 reviews in that area.

Reviewer status gives one ability to merge PRs directly into the project.

The first is making sure everyone's PRs are well-formed and conform to our standards. We could achieve this by having everyone submit PRs through our Physlib AI tool, where the AI guides the user toward producing pull requests that meet our conventions and are high quality from the start.
The second is having the AI review these pull requests: for simpler PRs the AI can approve them directly, while for cases where it's less certain or the PR is more complex, it can hand off to a human for further review

I'm not sure about forcing people to use the AI tool as I think that should really be a 'separate concept' from the main project itself. What maybe we can do though is come up with a PR template which we want people to follow.

One thing I think we could also do is the following: Currently the permissions for Physlib are such that to get a PR merged you need:

  • An approving review by someone who:
    • Is not the author
    • Who is what is called a codeowner by GithHub.
  • A maintainer to merge the PR.

Currently the codeowners are just the maintainers, we could either remove that condition entirely or expand codeownerpotentially automatically based on PRs merged.
I think I'm of the opinion that we potentially drop it entirely. The maintainer who merges it can make a judgement call whether they are satisfied with the review process.
(@ZhiKai Pong and @Daniel Morrison would be interested to hear your thoughts on the above).

Update (feel free to ignore my messages above)

Following the Physlib cafe I think here is where we landed with this is:

  • We will increase (fairly liberally) the number of people who can give an approving review, but will not open it up to anyone. Who gets an approving review will be at the discretion of the maintainers for the time being. A maintainer will still be required to merge the pull-request.

What this means in practice is: Creating a github team (maybe called physlib-reviewers) and setting them as the code-owners.

Would be helpful to know if people object or support this (either privately or publicly). If there is support I can implement it sometime next week.
(Will aim to set this up tomorrow, unless I hear anything otherwise)
(as you may well know, this is basically what we're doing in mathlib, with reviewers able to approve and then maintainers can glance through and merge)

@Kim Morrison Is it potential that we can have a team under leanprover-community called physlib-reviewers (as far as I can tell I don't have the permissions to set a team up)? Would it also be possible to have permissions to add people to that team (I think this requires a Team Maintainer role for that team)?

Sorry if you are not the correct person to ping regarding this :).

(Actually @Kevin Buzzard or @Johan Commelin or someone else with 'owner' status on leanprover-community- would you mind helping with this, as I just saw Kim might be offline for a number of days).

(Turns out I shouldn't actually need this - sorry for the ping)

I've been thinking about this but realized I forgot to actually respond! I think this is a good idea, I just have a couple of implementation questions/comments:

I think choosing a set of people who can give approving reviews is much better than letting anyone do it for a few reasons:

  • If it's anyone this could hypothetically be abused and someone approves their own work from another account
  • The amount of maintainer time to do the final pass is highly dependent on how much trust there is in the reviewer, if we select and trust them this does cut our workload but if it's a random person I would probably err on the side of redoing a lot of the review because I don't know their judgement
  • For practical purposes I think it's nice to have a set group of people so if something needs to change or we want to explain something it's easier to make sure we reach out to everyone in that group rather than disseminating info to the entire community

How (if at all) does this impact the rule that maintainers cannot approve their own work? Can they merge their own work if someone else provides an approving review?
sorry I was rather busy last week, I agree this is a good idea!

How (if at all) does this impact the rule that maintainers cannot approve their own work? Can they merge their own work if someone else provides an approving review?

Maintainers will not be able to approve their own work. I think with the naive implementation they would however be able to merge their own work. What are the thoughts on this?
Yeah, so someone else would review but they can final approve and merge. My inclination is that is fine and would help prevent maintainer PRs (really yours lol) from getting stuck, but I'm not sure.
Maybe we try it and see how it goes. But yeah - the key is that someone else (a designated reviewer) must look at any PR before merging
Agreed
(FYI currently changing the Rulesets on GitHub - this hopefully shouldn't effect anyone, but sorry if it does)

Ok, so turns out I didn't actually need an organisation team to do this:

How it works. Physlib now has two rulesets

  • "MasterBranchRules": Which says that every PR must have at least 1 review by someone other than the author with write access (= a reviewer). (This is the one we have always had).
  • "Merge restrictions": Which says no one can merge a pull request unless you are on a bypass list. The people on the by-pass list are the maintainers.

Reviewers should also be able to put labels on PRs without using comments. So should be able to assign a ready-to-merge label (unless we want another one like Mathlib called maintainer-merge?)
(Also just to reiterate what Kevin said above, I think this is just putting us more in line with the review policy of Mathlib).

Joseph Tooby-Smith said:

Reviewers should also be able to put labels on PRs without using comments. So should be able to assign a ready-to-merge label (unless we want another one like Mathlib called maintainer-merge?)

I don't think we can copy Mathlib too much here because the merge process is different. I would say keep ready-to-merge as is to keep the meaning literal and I think it's still useful in the case that a maintainer reviews another maintainer's work and it is then ready for the author to merge themselves. I would say we want another tag for reviewer approval so we can filter those that are just waiting for final approval. Maybe overkill for the moment but in the spirit of thinking about long-term scalability.

Mhm on second thought I tend to agree with @Daniel Morrison 's sentiment, at the moment, with the way the community is structured, the maintainer's PR's are a lot more complex/sensitive and is definetly worth a closer inspection by another maintainer, even if it slows things down at the moment. So maybe its worth introduding a new tag.

As a side note: in what way is the merge process different than mathlib's?

Mhm on second thought I tend to agree with @Daniel Morrison 's sentiment, at the moment, with the way the community is structured, the maintainer's PR's are a lot more complex/sensitive and is definetly worth a closer inspection by another maintainer, even if it slows things down at the moment. So maybe it's worth introduding a new tag.

I think this is slightly different from what Daniel is saying. There is the following situation that can occur

  • Maintainer A makes a pull-request -> Maintainer B reviews that.

Since both Maintainer A & B could in theory merge that PR, ready-to-merge is a signal from Maintainer B to Maintainer A that they can now that A can now merge it. We also have been using ready-to-merge as a bit of a safety net, to so we don't merge PRs directly after they are approved.

But I agree, we should introduce a tag which is reviewer-approved or similar.

I don't know a lot about it but there's an automatic system that handles much of the actual merging. Roughly speaking when a PR is approved the bot grabs the PR and commits it to a staging branch where it's tested and then batch merged into main. From the contributor side it doesn't really matter but the tags and such are specific to that process which we don't have so we can't copy the entire process

with the way the community is structured, the maintainer's PR's are a lot more complex/sensitive and is definetly worth a closer inspection by another maintainer, even if it slows things down at the moment. So

This is related to the following situation:

  • Maintainer A makes a pull-request -> Reviewer B reviews that PR

The question is whether we let Maintainer A now merge that PR, or do we require another maintainer to do it. I'm happy either way with this, but I actually don't know how to enforce it with the GitHub rule sets.

I think we can leave it up to maintainer discretion for the time being and see how it goes. So something small, unlikely to break just needs a reviewer's approval but a larger change it's perhaps for the best to get another maintaininer to double check your work.

@Joseph Tooby-Smith that makes soo much sense, sorry about the confusion. Not sure how we would deal with this, I'm not able to see the issue in letting the maintainer A in your analogy merge that PR.

But @Daniel Morrison you might be reffering to the bors bot that mathlib is using that does automatic merging.

Nathaneal Sajan said:

But Daniel Morrison you might be reffering to the bors bot that mathlib is using that does automatic merging.

Correct, what I meant is since we don't have bors our tags and workflow will be slightly different. The end result is basically the same but we have to take a little bit different path
(I think it is no longer recommended to use bors anymore on GitHub repos - as native GitHub features now cover most use-cases.)
Created a reviewer-approved label. Since reviewers have write access, they should be able to add it to a PR, but not an average user since it is not in the label via comment script.

Nathaneal Sajan said:

Joseph Tooby-Smith that makes soo much sense, sorry about the confusion. Not sure how we would deal with this, I'm not able to see the issue in letting the maintainer A in your analogy merge that PR.

For this, I think we keep things as they are, and iterate if things become a problem.
So @Daniel Morrison in theory ready-to-merge should be only used by maintainers, if I have understood things correctly? Not sure if there is a way to implement this directly.

I think so, since ready to merge to me implies all approvals are done and someone just needs to hit merge. At least for now I think we don't need to enforce this since maintainers and reviewers are chosen and trusted so I think it's fine to not mechanically restrict it from GitHubs end. Maybe would be nice to guard against mistakes but I don't think it's something that would prevent us from starting this

Also - wanted to clarify, a maintainer doesn’t need to also approve a PR which has already been approved by a reviewer. In a sense the action of merging is the final approval - if that changes anything. Although there is nothing stopping them, or in fact anyone else doing another complete review.

One thing I think it is worth doing is spelling out the details of each of the two task we have:

  • Reviewing
  • Merging

We have done reviewing but for merging maybe something along the lines of:

Consists of actually merging the PR into the project, along with checking that there are no outstanding comments or things which need addressing. The merger may also which to perform a further review of a PR if they deem it necessary.
